title: Reopening of the human visual critical period

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a controllable treatment that enables adults with long-standing amblyopia to recover substantial visual acuity in the affected eye and useful binocular vision, with lasting benefits after treatment ends and with the fellow eye remaining functional. Amblyopia involves impaired visual development: neural connections favor the fellow eye, and vision in the amblyopic eye can remain impaired after the original cause has been corrected. The target is recovery from this persistent developmental impairment.

Conceptual synthesis: reopening the visual critical period means restoring enough capacity for experience to reorganize the mature visual system that previously limited vision can develop substantially. A treatment might combine a temporary plasticity intervention with appropriate visual experience or rehabilitation. Durable clinical recovery would establish the therapeutic capability, but the title also carries a mechanistic hypothesis: demonstrating that the developmental critical period itself has reopened would require evidence beyond improved vision.

significance.text: If successful, the proposed treatment would make substantial recovery possible after a developmental visual deficit has persisted into adulthood. Restoring both acuity and stereopsis—the ability to judge depth from the two eyes together—would demonstrate recovery of complementary visual functions. Preserving fellow-eye function would also address the practical goal highlighted by the National Eye Institute: treating through the amblyopic eye without needing to interrupt vision in the better-seeing eye.

Scientific significance, as a conditional assessment: reproducible, durable adult recovery would establish substantial visual-system plasticity after developmental impairment. The central advance would be the magnitude, binocular scope and persistence of recovery. An improved training program could contribute to that outcome, but modest task performance gains alone would not establish the proposed capability, and functional success alone would not identify the biological mechanism.

Limits on the impact assessment: a successful amblyopia treatment could motivate investigation of plasticity in stroke rehabilitation or learning, but those applications would require their own mechanistic and functional demonstrations. The earlier comparison ranking amblyopia's human stakes below bilateral blinding disease is not established by the supplied evidence. Having a functional fellow eye is relevant to treatment design, but it does not by itself quantify disability or justify a general ranking of disease burden.

missing_breakthrough.text: The translational gap is a safe, controllable human intervention that produces durable recovery of acuity and binocular function in adults with residual amblyopia while preserving fellow-eye function. The December 2025 NEI account describes an adult-mouse result and identifies additional-species and eventual human testing as necessary next steps. That report supports a translational research goal; it does not establish a reliable human treatment or exhaustively determine which human treatments exist as of November 1, 2026.

Engineering and clinical synthesis: a temporary retinal intervention would need predictable depth and duration, reversibility, and acceptable retinal and visual safety. Researchers would need to establish how to guide the resulting plasticity toward useful vision, whether recovery of responses to one eye leads to coordinated binocular function, and whether gains persist after the intervention and rehabilitation stop. Animal restoration of a brain response does not settle these human functional questions.

Mechanistic synthesis: the critical-period interpretation requires distinguishing recovery through renewed developmental-like plasticity from compensation, task learning or other forms of adult adaptation. The earlier assertion that primary visual cortex cannot readily restore deprived-eye synaptic strength is too categorical for the retained evidence. The specific roles of synaptic recovery and thalamic bursting remain questions for verification rather than established explanations in this record.

current_state.text: The NEI report dated December 1, 2025 describes an adult-mouse experiment in which temporary, reversible anesthesia of the amblyopic retina restored the brain's visual response to that eye. This is an animal proof of principle for recovery after developmental impairment. The report places testing in additional species and ultimately humans ahead; it does not demonstrate restored human acuity, human stereopsis or clinical completion of the proposed innovation.

The earlier research attributed a November 2025 Cell Reports study to Echavarri-Leet, Chauhan, Cramer, Fong and Bear, and described restored cortical synaptic strength after prolonged monocular deprivation with thalamic bursting required for recovery. The supplied review found only redirect text in the retained DOI artifact, rather than article content or the claimed DOAJ abstract. Its authorship, publication details and specific mechanistic findings therefore remain unverified here. The independently retained NEI account supports the narrower animal-response result above; the missing article content is not evidence that the more detailed findings are false.

The NEI article makes a categorical claim that existing interventions are effective only in infancy and early childhood. The earlier research challenged that claim by describing partial adult gains from perceptual training, dichoptic stimulation and neuromodulation, generally in small studies with short follow-up, and cited a purported September 2025 Vision Research review. However, the retained review DOI artifact also contains only redirect text. These materials establish neither the categorical childhood-only claim nor the proposed correction's treatment effects, sample sizes or follow-up pattern. They also do not establish whether those interventions reset a developmental window.

Evidence limitation: the earlier research mentioned a 2024 fluoxetine-plus-patching trial and a secondary description of a modest additional acuity gain. Neither the primary paper nor the secondary report is supplied, so the trial's design, outcome and clinical significance cannot be determined here. More broadly, the supplied bounded search record is empty. The dated animal result remains relevant, but this record cannot establish the field's clinical status through November 1, 2026 or support an exhaustive claim that no human method reliably restores normal acuity and stereopsis.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: enroll adults with stable residual amblyopia after appropriate optical correction in a controlled trial. Demonstrate near-normal acuity in the amblyopic eye together with measurable, functionally meaningful stereopsis, while preserving fellow-eye function. Prespecify the acuity and stereopsis thresholds, the control condition, safety outcomes and the proportion of participants required to meet the combined endpoint. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established clinical standards.
completion_criteria.label: Near-normal acuity and meaningful stereopsis with preserved fellow-eye function

completion_criteria.text: Proposed magnitude and durability requirements: an acuity improvement of only one or two chart lines would not meet this record's intended breakthrough threshold, although it could still be clinically useful. Recovery should persist for a prespecified period after the plasticity intervention ends, with rehabilitation exposure and any ongoing maintenance treatment documented. The current inputs do not justify choosing a numerical definition of near-normal vision or a particular follow-up duration; these require explicit justification in the trial protocol.
completion_criteria.label: Recovery exceeds two chart lines and persists after intervention

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: confirm the combined acuity and binocular benefit in independent cohorts or centers, distinguish generalized visual improvement from practice on the tested tasks, and report outcomes across relevant ages, amblyopia causes and baseline severities. Document adverse effects, treatment burden and preservation of fellow-eye vision. Finite trials would establish the demonstrated breadth of treatment, with nonresponders and excluded populations defining important limits.
completion_criteria.label: Independent cohorts reproduce generalized visual recovery and define treatment limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mechanistic demonstration: pair clinical recovery with evidence that the intervention restores a developmentally relevant capacity for visual reorganization. Converging physiological and functional measurements should distinguish that explanation from ordinary adult learning or compensation. Meeting the clinical endpoints would establish a recovery capability even if its mechanism remained uncertain; attributing it specifically to reopening the human visual critical period would require this additional evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Clinical recovery accompanies restored developmental plasticity beyond learning or compensation

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: OPH-01, Retinotopic reconnection of retinal ganglion cell axons to brain targets, overlaps in the need for useful organization of signals reaching the brain, but concerns rebuilding anatomical connections. OPH-05, Patterned vision from the brain when the eye cannot send signals, overlaps in central visual processing and adaptation, but concerns generating patterned vision through a brain interface. OPH-09 targets recovery from developmental amblyopia; it does not itself establish axon reconnection or an artificial source of visual signals.

Roster-based comparison: OPH-02, Biological reconstruction of foveal cones, RPE, and their blood supply; OPH-07, One programmable repair for many photoreceptor and RPE gene defects; and OPH-08, Reperfusion of established retinal capillary dropout, address retinal tissue, genetic or vascular problems. Restoring retinal input could create a setting in which visual-system adaptation matters, but OPH-09 does not rebuild those tissues, correct their gene defects or restore their circulation. Any combined benefit remains a separate hypothesis.

Roster-based comparison: OPH-03, Reversal of established cataract without removing the lens, and OPH-04, A manufactured cornea that clears vascularized stromal opacity, concern clearing optical obstacles. OPH-06, A closed-loop control that sets axial eye growth, concerns controlling eye growth. OPH-09 addresses persistent developmental visual impairment after the original cause has been corrected. Improving optics or growth control and recovering amblyopic function are distinct capabilities.

Roster-based comparison: OPH-10, Arrest of glaucomatous ganglion-cell death when pressure is not the lever, and OPH-11, Prevention of progression from early or intermediate AMD to late AMD, focus on preventing further disease damage. OPH-09 focuses on restoring function after abnormal visual development. Plasticity-based rehabilitation could conceivably complement disease control, but it would not by itself establish ganglion-cell protection or prevention of AMD progression. Each roster entry retains its separate target and completion criteria.

unresolved_issues: The Cell Reports article's identity, authorship, November 2025 publication details, experimental scope, synaptic findings and thalamic-bursting requirement remain unverified from the retained redirect artifact.
The Vision Research review's identity, September 2025 publication details and evidence for adult treatment gains, sample sizes and follow-up remain unverified.
Neither a primary nor secondary report for the described 2024 fluoxetine-plus-patching trial is supplied.
The available evidence cannot resolve the NEI article's categorical childhood-only treatment assertion or the earlier research's clinical-literature rebuttal.
No bounded search evidence establishes clinical developments through November 1, 2026.
Numerical acuity and stereopsis thresholds, follow-up duration, acceptable maintenance treatment and safety boundaries remain to be justified for the proposed demonstration.
The human applicability, durability and safety of temporary amblyopic-retina inactivation, and its ability to restore useful binocular function, remain undetermined here.
The mechanistic evidence required to attribute recovery specifically to reopening the developmental critical period remains to be defined and demonstrated.

brief.title: Lasting adult recovery from poorly developed vision
possible: Adults with amblyopia—vision that stayed weak because it developed abnormally—could gain sharp sight in the affected eye and use both eyes together to judge depth. The gains would last after treatment ends, while the better-seeing eye remains functional.
why: People whose visual difficulties began in childhood could recover complementary abilities: seeing detail and judging depth with both eyes. Substantial, lasting recovery would also show how much the mature visual system can reorganize after disrupted development.

sources.who: Echavarri-Leet, Chauhan, Cramer, Fong and Bear
sources.showed: An animal study of recovery in brain connections after prolonged deprivation of vision in one eye.
sources.cited_for: It concerns recovery in the brain's visual system after disrupted development.
sources.not_established: It does not establish lasting recovery of sharp sight and coordinated vision in adult humans.

sources.who: Mark Bear's lab at MIT's Picower Institute and collaborators
sources.showed: In adult mice, temporarily numbing the retina—the eye's light-sensitive tissue—in the affected eye restored the brain's visual response to it.
sources.quote: if the retina of the amblyopic eye is temporarily and reversibly anesthetized just for a couple of days, the brain’s visual response to the eye can be restored even in adulthood.
sources.cited_for: The mouse result supports testing whether a temporary intervention can restore vision after disrupted development.
sources.not_established: A restored brain response in mice does not establish safe, lasting recovery of sharp sight or depth perception in humans.

sources.who: Authors of the Vision Research review
sources.showed: A review concerning treatments for amblyopia in adults.
sources.cited_for: It concerns attempts to improve adult vision through training and stimulation.
sources.not_established: It does not establish that treatment restores the developmental capacity to reorganize vision.

shown: Mark Bear's MIT team restored the brain's response to the affected eye in adult mice by temporarily numbing that eye's retina. This provides an animal proof of principle; human recovery of sharp sight and useful vision from both eyes remains to be demonstrated.
missing: A safe, controllable human treatment must produce substantial recovery while preserving the better-seeing eye's function.
Recovery must include useful depth perception from both eyes and persist after treatment and rehabilitation stop.
Independent studies must reproduce benefits beyond improvement on practiced tasks.
Biological measurements must distinguish restored developmental flexibility from ordinary adult learning or compensation.

milestones.label: Near-normal sight and depth perception with both eyes protected
milestones.explanation: A controlled adult trial would have to show near-normal sharpness and meaningful depth perception from both eyes, preserving the better eye's function. This would establish recovery of complementary visual abilities.

milestones.label: Recovery beyond two chart lines that lasts
milestones.explanation: Sharpness would have to improve by more than two eye-chart lines and persist for a justified period after the intervention ends. This would establish the required scale and durability of recovery.

milestones.label: Independent studies reproduce broad recovery and define treatment limits
milestones.explanation: Independent groups would have to reproduce gains beyond practiced tasks and report outcomes across ages, causes and severities, including harms. This would establish who benefits and the treatment's limits.

milestones.label: Recovery accompanies restored developmental flexibility
milestones.explanation: Clinical recovery would have to accompany measurements showing renewed developmental capacity to reorganize vision, distinguishable from learning or compensation. This would support reopening the childhood window for visual development.

uncertain: Can temporarily numbing the affected retina safely restore lasting, coordinated vision in humans?
What thresholds for sharpness, depth perception and lasting benefit should count, and how much maintenance treatment is acceptable?
Which measurements would establish that the childhood window for visual development has reopened?

page.title: Reopening the human visual critical period
page.definition: A treatment restores the capacity of adult visual circuits to reorganize through experience as they do during childhood. In adults with amblyopia, a lasting visual deficit caused by abnormal visual development, this restores the ability to resolve fine detail and to perceive depth from differences between the two eyes’ images, without lasting loss in the fellow eye. Visual training can already improve adult stereoacuity. Reopening requires evidence that the recovery depends on developmental plasticity.

goal.need: Glasses can correct blur while amblyopia persists, and patching works best in childhood. Better vision in adulthood could help people judge depth at work and in daily life, and leave them with more usable sight if the better eye loses vision. Among 5,220 adults aged 55 or older in Rotterdam, the 192 with amblyopia had 2.6 times the risk of bilateral visual impairment over a median 6.5 years (95% CI 1.4–4.5). Whether adult treatment reduces that risk remains unknown.

figures.caption: Five-year cumulative incidence of bilateral visual impairment in the Rotterdam Study.
figures.note: Impairment meant best-corrected decimal acuity below 0.5 in the better eye, without improvement at subsequent examinations. These are observational cohort risks.

statements.quote: Develop and test pharmacological and behavioral methods for induction and improvement of plasticity in adults
statements.context: A research priority for strabismus, amblyopia and disorders involving central visual processing.

statements.body: The Lasker/IRRF Initiative for Innovation in Vision Science
statements.quote: guide clinical trials by enhancing plasticity in post-critical period visual cortex in humans.
statements.context: The critical-period discussion group set this goal in chapter 3 of Amblyopia: Challenges and Opportunities and published its recommendations in 2018.

completion.title: Replicated human studies establish lasting visual recovery caused by reinstated developmental plasticity.
completion.criterion: A randomized trial in adults aged ≥18 years with residual amblyopia accounts for improvement from refractive correction and shows superior gains in best-corrected amblyopic-eye acuity and stereoacuity versus control. An acuity responder gains ≥10 ETDRS letters, a decrease of ≥0.2 logMAR. Both benefits persist 12–24 months after treatment ends without persistent fellow-eye loss. Independent replication of physiological evidence establishes that reinstated developmental-like, experience-dependent cortical plasticity mediates recovery beyond task learning or compensation alone.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis; no outside body was found to define this combined human completion test.
completion.basis: The adult fluoxetine trial defines the acuity response. The BRAVO study identifies improvement from optical correction as a separate treatment effect. The Cochrane protocol specifies the long-term assessment window for acuity and stereoacuity. The Lasker/IRRF recommendations distinguish developmental from residual adult plasticity. The combined clinical and mechanistic criterion is an Atlas synthesis.

milestones.title: Seven days of monocular deprivation shift adult mouse cortical responses toward the open eye.
milestones.criterion: Measure the relative cortical response to each eye before and after seven days of monocular deprivation in treated adult mice and age-matched untreated controls. Treatment restores a shift in ocular dominance toward the open eye at an age when the deprivation alone produces little or no shift.
milestones.set_by: Steinzeig and colleagues, adult-mouse ocular-dominance protocol, Methods section 2.4.
milestones.threshold_quote: To test for cortical plasticity, the mice were monocularly deprived for one week in all groups.

milestones.title: Treatment reverses the deprivation-induced shift in mouse cortical eye preference at one week.
milestones.criterion: After monocular deprivation from postnatal day 26 to day 47, reopen the eye and assess cortical responses to stimulation of each eye on day 54. The ocular-dominance ratio must shift back toward the normally reared reference relative to untreated deprived mice. Compare the groups using the animal as the unit of analysis.
milestones.set_by: Echavarri-Leet and colleagues, Cell Reports 2025, Figure 4 and STAR Methods; this operational recovery test concerns mouse deprivation amblyopia.
milestones.threshold_quote: restores a normal ocular dominance ratio when assessed 1 week later

milestones.title: An adult’s amblyopic eye gains at least 10 ETDRS letters from baseline.
milestones.criterion: Measure amblyopic-eye acuity on the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study chart before and after treatment. An individual responds if the eye reads at least 10 additional letters, equivalent to two lines or a decrease of at least 0.2 logMAR.
milestones.set_by: Huttunen and colleagues, adult-amblyopia phase 2 trial, Methods: Clinical assessments; the authors' definition of clinically relevant acuity improvement.
milestones.threshold_quote: a 0.2 or greater decrease in the logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution (logMAR) visual acuity

milestones.title: A randomized adult-amblyopia trial shows greater acuity improvement with treatment than with placebo.
milestones.criterion: In a randomized, masked adult-amblyopia trial, compare the change from baseline in amblyopic-eye logMAR acuity between an added intervention and placebo, with the same background treatment in both groups. The mean change must favor the intervention at the specified endpoint, with P < 0.05 for the between-group comparison.
milestones.set_by: Randomized placebo-controlled adult-amblyopia trials of Huttunen and colleagues and Mirmohammadsadeghi and colleagues.
milestones.threshold_quote: P values of less than 0.05 were considered to indicate statistical significance.

milestones.title: Adults retain controlled acuity and stereopsis benefits 12–24 months after amblyopia treatment ends.
milestones.criterion: In a controlled adult study, compare change from baseline in best-corrected amblyopic-eye acuity and stereoacuity 12–24 months after treatment ends. Both outcomes must retain a benefit over control. Measure fellow-eye acuity separately to establish that treatment has caused no persistent loss.
milestones.set_by: Atlas synthesis. The Cochrane protocol specifies both long-term outcomes. The AAO pediatric guideline calls for monitoring acuity in each eye. No outside body defines the combined adult success test.

milestones.title: Adult rats resolve finer gratings through the previously deprived eye after treatment.
milestones.criterion: Following developmental monocular deprivation, test the previously deprived eye on a two-alternative forced-choice grating detection task. Its spatial-frequency threshold must improve relative to the control condition with the same visual training. Score the threshold in cycles per degree at the highest spatial frequency with at least 60% correct choices in two consecutive blocks.
milestones.set_by: Eaton, Sheehan and Quinlan, adult-rat visual detection protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: The highest spatial frequency with performance of ≥60% correct choices on two consecutive blocks of trials is reported as daily detection threshold.

milestones.title: An adult’s Randot stereoacuity threshold falls fourfold or becomes measurable for the first time.
milestones.criterion: Use the Randot Preschool Test at baseline and at the outcome visit. Count a response when the smallest detectable binocular disparity falls to one-quarter of baseline or less, or when a participant with no detectable stereopsis at baseline achieves a measurable threshold.
milestones.set_by: BRAVO Study Team, optical-treatment study, Figure 3C.
milestones.threshold_quote: A 2-octaves (4-fold) decrease in threshold or a change from no detectable stereopsis at baseline to a measurable threshold at the outcome visit

not_found: No accepted human assay or consensus pass criterion for reopening the visual critical period was found.
No study meeting the combined long-term clinical and mechanistic completion test was identified.
ClinicalTrials.gov pages for NCT02685423, NCT07764198 and NCT07846397 returned page shells without readable study details.
The supplied Vision Research DOI did not yield readable article text.
No statement opposing pursuit of adult critical-period reopening was identified in NEI priorities, Lasker/IRRF recommendations or AAO guidance.

results.finding: In adult mice (sample size unreported), the brain’s response to the amblyopic eye recovered after a couple of days of retinal anesthesia.
results.detail: The article identifies the underlying study as published in Cell Reports.
results.quote: if the retina of the amblyopic eye is temporarily and reversibly anesthetized just for a couple of days, the brain’s visual response to the eye can be restored even in adulthood.

results.finding: Adult mice (8 fluoxetine-treated, 5 controls) showed a 0.21-point shift in ocular dominance index toward the open eye with treatment.
results.detail: The shift was driven mainly by a weaker response to the closed eye. A separate cohort tested after a one-week fluoxetine washout (n = 5) showed no shift toward the open eye.
results.quote: The IOS data demonstrated that after 12 weeks of fluoxetine (80 mg/L in the drinking water), closing the eye for 7 days resulted in a shift in OD from 0.2 ± 0.03 to −0.01 ± 0.03 (one‐way ANOVA, Sidak‐corrected). This was indicative of an ipsilateral (open) eye dominance.

results.finding: Adult wild-type mice given fluoxetine (n=7, water controls n=8) shifted cortical dominance toward the open eye (P<0.0001).
results.detail: Fluoxetine began three weeks before deprivation and continued through it. The P values describe within-group changes from baseline.
results.quote: Flx permits MD to shift the ODI towards the non-deprived eye in V1 of WT mice, but fails to do so in hPV-TrkB CKO mice

results.finding: Adult optoTrkB mice (n=8, unstimulated controls n=5) shifted cortical eye preference back during reverse occlusion (P=0.0201).
results.detail: The reversal occurred during a second deprivation period. The reported P value tests the change within the stimulated group.

results.finding: At least 12 of 37 adults with anisometropic amblyopia met the ETDRS responder threshold.
results.detail: The anisometropic count is a lower bound derived from the pooled results. The paper gives no exact responder count by cause.
results.quote: Nine subjects (42.8%) in the fluoxetine group and eight subjects (40.0%) in the control group improved visual acuity ≥0.2 logMAR units at the primary efficacy endpoint

results.finding: In 42 adults with amblyopia, predominantly anisometropic, the acuity comparison gave P = 0.524.
results.detail: The paper reports no separate treatment effect for the anisometropic subgroup.
results.quote: At the primary endpoint, the mean treatment group difference in visual acuity improvement was only 0.027 logMAR units (95% CI: −0.057 to 0.110; p = 0.524).

results.finding: Among 34 adults with amblyopia who completed follow-up, 15 retained the ETDRS responder gain.
results.detail: The follow-up counts were pooled across causes. At least 10 responders had anisometropic amblyopia because only 5 participants in the entire trial had other etiologies.
results.quote: visual gains of at least 0.2 logMAR units persisted in many subjects in both groups [9 of 20 fluoxetine subjects (45.0%), 6 of 14 control subjects (42.9%);

results.detail: The case was represented in the pooled cohort. Its sample size and treatment effect were not reported separately.
results.quote: mean logMAR improvement was significantly higher in the fluoxetine group than in the placebo group (P = 0.04).

results.finding: Adults with anisometropic or strabismic amblyopia (n=55) had greater pooled acuity improvement with fluoxetine than placebo (P = 0.04).
results.detail: The case was represented in the pooled cohort. Its sample size and treatment effect were not reported separately.

results.quote: The mean logMAR visual acuity of the amblyopic eye improved by 0.20 ± 0.24 (0-0.8) in the fluoxetine group (P < 0.001) and by 0.08 ± 0.15 (0-0.7) in the placebo group (P = 0.01)

results.finding: Adult mice (n = 14) shifted cortical ocular dominance toward the open eye after 3 days of deprivation only with REST knockdown.
results.detail: The shift involved a weaker cortical response to the deprived eye.
results.quote: While in our adult naive and ΔCre-transduced controls, the 3-day MD was unable to modify the C/I ratio, REST knocked down mice experienced a significant change in OD toward the non-deprived ipsilateral eye

results.finding: Developmentally deprived mice (n = 19) recovered cortical ocular dominance after 15 days of reverse suture only with REST knockdown.
results.detail: Recovery reflected a stronger cortical response to the previously deprived eye.

results.finding: Among two adults with strabismic amblyopia, P5 gained the equivalent of 20 ETDRS letters in the amblyopic eye after citalopram plus patching.
results.detail: Tables 1 and 2 link P5’s strabismic classification to the individual acuity result. The seven-participant trial found no statistically significant difference between the active and placebo blocks.

results.finding: Of 6 adults with mixed strabismic and anisometropic amblyopia, 2 met the 10-letter amblyopic-eye gain threshold at week 24.
results.detail: The responder count was calculated by matching amblyopia type in Table 1 to individual acuity changes in Table 2. Treatment was tapered after week 12 and discontinued before the week 24 assessment.

results.finding: One adult with mixed strabismic and anisometropic amblyopia (n=1) gained 32 E-ETDRS letters in the amblyopic eye.
results.detail: The comparison uses Table 1’s initial evaluation as baseline. At three months, acuity had declined to 73 letters, still 24 above that baseline. The patient was subsequently lost to follow-up.

results.finding: Threshold reached 400 arcseconds in one adult with strabismic amblyopia in a three-adult case series.
results.detail: She discontinued therapy when she relocated. The 400-arcsecond result was recorded before she was lost to follow-up.

case_label = "Cause". Reason: Cause is the prespecified clinical subgroup that distinguishes these four forms of unilateral amblyopia.

definition = "A treatment restores the capacity of adult visual circuits to reorganize through experience as they do during childhood. In adults with amblyopia, a lasting visual deficit caused by abnormal visual development, this restores the ability to resolve fine detail and to perceive depth from differences between the two eyes\u2019 images, without lasting loss in the fellow eye. Visual training can already improve adult stereoacuity. Reopening requires evidence that the recovery depends on developmental plasticity.". Reason: The definition needs to distinguish reinstated developmental plasticity from the recovery already documented after adult visual training.

goal.need = "Glasses can correct blur while amblyopia persists, and patching works best in childhood. Better vision in adulthood could help people judge depth at work and in daily life, and leave them with more usable sight if the better eye loses vision. Among 5,220 adults aged 55 or older in Rotterdam, the 192 with amblyopia had 2.6 times the risk of bilateral visual impairment over a median 6.5 years (95% CI 1.4\u20134.5). Whether adult treatment reduces that risk remains unknown.". Reason: The risk estimate gains clinical meaning when paired with the limits of childhood treatment and the everyday uses of recovered vision.

add statement by The Lasker/IRRF Initiative for Innovation in Vision Science, 2017: "guide clinical trials by enhancing plasticity in post-critical period visual cortex in humans.". Reason: The original report identifies enhanced plasticity in the human visual cortex as a goal for clinical trials.

edit completion: criterion = "A randomized trial in adults aged \u226518 years with residual amblyopia accounts for improvement from refractive correction and shows superior gains in best-corrected amblyopic-eye acuity and stereoacuity versus control. An acuity responder gains \u226510 ETDRS letters, a decrease of \u22650.2 logMAR. Both benefits persist 12\u201324 months after treatment ends without persistent fellow-eye loss. Independent replication of physiological evidence establishes that reinstated developmental-like, experience-dependent cortical plasticity mediates recovery beyond task learning or compensation alone."; basis = "The adult fluoxetine trial defines the acuity response. The BRAVO study identifies improvement from optical correction as a separate treatment effect. The Cochrane protocol specifies the long-term assessment window for acuity and stereoacuity. The Lasker/IRRF recommendations distinguish developmental from residual adult plasticity. The combined clinical and mechanistic criterion is an Atlas synthesis."; refs = [3, 5, 6, 15, 17]. Reason: The trial must account for improvement from optical correction itself, and the basis should identify which parts of the combined test come from external protocols.
add case "Strabismic". Reason: The adult review protocol treats amblyopia caused by eye misalignment as a distinct subgroup.
add case "Anisometropic". Reason: The protocol distinguishes unequal refractive error between the eyes, and an adult trial found a cause-specific treatment response.
add case "Mixed strabismic and anisometropic". Reason: The protocol identifies coexisting eye misalignment and unequal refractive error as a separate subgroup.
add case "Deprivation". Reason: The protocol distinguishes deprivation amblyopia, the form modeled by blocking patterned vision during development.

edit m1: title = "Seven days of monocular deprivation shift adult mouse cortical responses toward the open eye."; criterion = "Measure the relative cortical response to each eye before and after seven days of monocular deprivation in treated adult mice and age-matched untreated controls. Treatment restores a shift in ocular dominance toward the open eye at an age when the deprivation alone produces little or no shift."; set_by = "Steinzeig and colleagues, adult-mouse ocular-dominance protocol, Methods section 2.4."; set_by_kind = "protocol"; threshold_quote = "To test for cortical plasticity, the mice were monocularly deprived for one week in all groups."; threshold_ref = 8; refs = [3, 8]. Reason: Seven days is a condition of the adult-mouse protocol, and the observed index values belong with the result.

edit m2: title = "Treatment reverses the deprivation-induced shift in mouse cortical eye preference at one week."; criterion = "After monocular deprivation from postnatal day 26 to day 47, reopen the eye and assess cortical responses to stimulation of each eye on day 54. The ocular-dominance ratio must shift back toward the normally reared reference relative to untreated deprived mice. Compare the groups using the animal as the unit of analysis."; threshold_quote = "restores a normal ocular dominance ratio when assessed 1 week later"; threshold_ref = 7; refs = [7]. Reason: The criterion should specify the recording endpoint and both comparison groups without embedding sample sizes or treating a nonsignificant difference as equivalence.

add milestone after m2: "Adult rats resolve finer gratings through the previously deprived eye after treatment.". Reason: A cortical eye-preference ratio cannot establish how much detail the animal can see through the previously deprived eye.

edit m3: title = "An adult\u2019s amblyopic eye gains at least 10 ETDRS letters from baseline."; criterion = "Measure amblyopic-eye acuity on the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study chart before and after treatment. An individual responds if the eye reads at least 10 additional letters, equivalent to two lines or a decrease of at least 0.2 logMAR."; refs = [5]. Reason: The responder test is an individual change from baseline, with better acuity corresponding to a lower logMAR value.

add milestone after m3: "An adult’s Randot stereoacuity threshold falls fourfold or becomes measurable for the first time.". Reason: The BRAVO study defines an individual stereoacuity response, including how to score an adult with no measurable stereopsis at baseline.

edit m4: criterion = "In a randomized, masked adult-amblyopia trial, compare the change from baseline in amblyopic-eye logMAR acuity between an added intervention and placebo, with the same background treatment in both groups. The mean change must favor the intervention at the specified endpoint, with P < 0.05 for the between-group comparison."; set_by = "Randomized placebo-controlled adult-amblyopia trials of Huttunen and colleagues and Mirmohammadsadeghi and colleagues."; set_by_kind = "community_convention"; threshold_quote = "P values of less than 0.05 were considered to indicate statistical significance."; threshold_ref = 5; refs = [5, 9]. Reason: The efficacy criterion is the between-group difference in acuity change, which can be stated independently of the two fluoxetine trials’ conflicting results.

edit m5: criterion = "In a controlled adult study, compare change from baseline in best-corrected amblyopic-eye acuity and stereoacuity 12\u201324 months after treatment ends. Both outcomes must retain a benefit over control. Measure fellow-eye acuity separately to establish that treatment has caused no persistent loss."; set_by = "Atlas synthesis. The Cochrane protocol specifies both long-term outcomes. The AAO pediatric guideline calls for monitoring acuity in each eye. No outside body defines the combined adult success test."; set_by_kind = "atlas"; refs = [6, 15]. Reason: Cochrane specifies when and what to measure, while the favorable effect and fellow-eye safety requirement belong to the Atlas synthesis.
